Executive Interpretation

The reporting-country median in 2023 is low by global standards, but the mean remains much higher because a small set of countries and territories record very high homicide rates. The answer to whether the world is becoming safer is therefore conditional: the median country looks relatively safer, while acute, geographically concentrated violence continues to dominate the global average and policy burden.

Central tendency improved unevenlyThe unweighted mean rate fell from the 2000s to the 2010s, while the 2020s are nearly flat relative to the 2010s in the available data.
Gender disparity is structuralIn 2023, the mean male homicide rate is 14.97 versus 2.21 for females among paired reporting countries.
Coverage limits inferenceOnly 41.8% of ever-reporting total-rate countries have 2023 total-rate observations; missing rows were not imputed.

1. Global Homicide Rate Overview

The global overview uses observations where sex = both and age_group = ALL, providing the cleanest country-level total homicide-rate panel. The file contains 4,215 such country-year observations across 201 countries/territories from 1990 to 2023.

From 1990 to 2023, the unweighted median changed from 3.35 to 1.84 per 100,000 (-45.1%), while the mean changed from 6.33 to 8.29 (+30.9%). The gap between mean and median in recent years signals a skewed distribution: most reporting countries sit at comparatively low rates, but a smaller number of high-rate countries pull the average upward.

2. Regional & Country-Level Comparison

The dataset does not include a region field and the rule prohibits adding external classifications. Geographic patterns are therefore described from country and territory names only. The highest rates in 2023 are concentrated in Caribbean and Latin American countries/territories among those reporting that year, while the lowest rates are largely in East Asian, European, and small-state contexts.

3. Gender Disparity in Homicide Victimization

Gender disparity is one of the clearest patterns in the file. In 2023, among 81 countries with both male and female total-rate observations, the mean male homicide rate is 14.97 per 100,000 and the mean female rate is 2.21, yielding a male-to-female ratio of 6.78×. The median country-level ratio is lower, at 3.17×, indicating that extremely high male rates in some countries raise the global mean ratio.

Policy implication: homicide prevention strategies need a strong focus on male victimization, particularly young and working-age men, without obscuring targeted risks faced by women in specific local contexts.

4. Age Group Analysis

Age-group rows are available only for male and female records in this file; there are no sex = both age-specific rates. The analysis below therefore uses each country-sex-age group’s most recent observation and reports the median across countries, avoiding interpolation across reporting gaps.

For males, the highest median most-recent age-specific rate is in the 30–44 group at 5.15 per 100,000 across 97 reporting countries. For females, the highest median is in the 30–44 group at 1.32 per 100,000 across 97 reporting countries.

The age pattern reinforces the gender finding: male rates rise sharply from adolescence into young adulthood, while female rates are lower and flatter across age groups in median terms.

5. Notable Country-Level Trends & Outliers

Country-level outliers are measured as the absolute change between the first and latest available total-rate observation, restricted to countries with at least 8 observations and a span of at least 15 years. This rule reduces noise from very short series while preserving the unbalanced-panel structure.

6. Data Limitations & Policy Recommendations

Data limitations

  • Unbalanced panel: country reporting varies by year; 162 countries report in the best-covered year (2008), versus 84 in the lowest-covered year (2023).
  • Partial latest-year coverage: 2023 has 84 total-rate reporting countries, or 41.8% of countries with at least one total-rate observation.
  • No imputation: absent rows remain absent; all KPIs and charts use observed values only.
  • Limited region analysis: no region column is provided, so no external regional grouping is introduced.
  • Age data constraint: age-specific rows are available for male/female records, not for both-sex totals.
  • UK caveat: as documented in the source brief, UK data refer to England and Wales only, with Scotland and Northern Ireland potentially reported separately.

Policy recommendations grounded in the observed data

  • Prioritize high-rate outliers: direct violence-prevention resources and international cooperation toward countries and territories with the highest observed rates and fastest deteriorations.
  • Target male victimization: build prevention programs around the consistently elevated male homicide risk, especially ages where male median rates peak.
  • Maintain gains in improving countries: countries with large declines provide candidates for deeper qualitative review, using external policy/context data outside this report’s scope.
  • Invest in reporting completeness: trend monitoring is weakened when latest-year coverage is below half of ever-reporting countries; harmonized annual reporting should be treated as a public-safety infrastructure priority.
  • Use mean and median together: median trends describe the typical reporting country, while mean trends identify the influence of high-violence outliers; both are necessary for allocation decisions.

Methodological Notes

All statistics are derived directly from /app/benchmark/data.csv. The principal global and country comparisons use sex = both and age_group = ALL. Gender analysis uses paired country-years with male and female ALL observations. Age analysis uses most recent country-sex-age observations because total-population age rows are not present. Averages are unweighted across reporting countries; the dataset does not include population counts for population-weighted global rates.

Generated as a self-contained HTML report with embedded base64 chart images. No external sources or fabricated values are included.
